title: GraphBEAT: Graph-based Bucketized Event Aggregation Over Time for Early Risk Stratification of Gastrointestinal Cancers

summary: Weight-space learning across architectures requires representations that respect parameter symmetries and scale to large networks. Existing equivariant tensor encoders require architecture-specific symmetry specifications, while neuron graphs make global attention costly. We introduce a typed graph organized around shared coordinate-permutation actions. Its nodes, called interfaces, represent coordinate spaces whose bound tensor axes must be permuted jointly; operation occurrences, called modules, form typed hyperedges. A compiler derives this graph from supported PyTorch models, with exact recovery of the permutation factors defined by its constraints. The Universal Weight Encoder (UWE) combines local equivariant updates to parameter features with global attention over invariant interface summaries. The small number of interfaces makes global attention practical, and a single encoder processes different supported architectures. UWE is competitive with architecture-specific state-of-the-art methods on established benchmarks. On a new zoo of 1,200 transformers spanning 100 architectures, it outperforms the evaluated baselines at ranking networks within unseen architectures, including architectures larger than those used for training, while using substantially less memory.
title: Interfaces and Modules: A Scalable Representation for Weight-Space Learning across Architectures

summary: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.
title: CoWorld Reasoner: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning with the Evolving Video World Model-Driven Harness

summary: Learning intrinsic dynamics---the relationship between actions and their consequences---is essential for world models. However, visual variations unrelated to the underlying control process can obscure this relationship in learned representations. We investigate the connection between action predictability, defined as the ability to reconstruct an action from consecutive latent states, and the preservation of intrinsic dynamics. Our central hypothesis is that encouraging action predictability discourages representations from discarding the distinctions between different actions and their consequences. We provide two complementary forms of evidence for this connection. Theoretically, we derive a positive lower bound on squared inverse prediction error when the encoder merges distinguishable outcomes of different actions from the same state and appearance, and show that forward prediction can still be exact on those transitions. Empirically, controlled appearance-diversity comparisons, supervision interventions, and latent probes support the role of action prediction in preserving control-relevant transition information. We instantiate action predictability with Concat IDM, which predicts actions from concatenated latent states and updates the shared encoder using action labels already available in offline trajectories, without changing the test-time planner. Across three independent training runs on Push-T with 24 appearances, Concat IDM increases planning success from 9.1% to 77.2%; its paired improvement is 52.9 percentage points larger than that observed with a single appearance. Together, these findings support action predictability as an inductive bias toward intrinsic dynamics and demonstrate the practical benefits of Concat IDM for latent planning under visual diversity.
title: Learning Intrinsic Dynamics in Latent World Models

summary: Biological intelligence continually adapts to new information while retaining prior skills through localized plasticity. In contrast, continual learning in large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. A promising direction is to identify functionally specialized subnetworks within LLMs that enable targeted and resource-efficient adaptation. Using gradient-attribution profiling, we localize cognition-associated functional subnetworks exhibiting extremely low mutual overlap. Building on this finding, we propose Function-isolated Memory-Efficient Optimization (CiMEO), a continual learning framework that routes each training example to its corresponding functional subnetwork, restricting parameter updates and optimizer states to selected regions. Across 1.4 million sequential instructions, CiMEO achieves the highest average performance among the compared methods on five generative benchmarks spanning programming, examination-style tasks, and mathematical reasoning, while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Subspace-overlap and principal-angle analyses further indicate that localized updates help preserve pre-trained representations, highlighting functional subnetwork localization as a practical approach to efficient and stable continual learning in LLMs.
title: Functional Subnetwork Localization for Efficient Continual Learning in Large Language Models

summary: Reducing memory use in large language model (LLM) training is an ongoing challenge. Activation checkpointing saves memory by recomputation, while lossy compression changes the stored activations. The reemergence of sparse $\relu$ and $\relu^2$ activations creates a third opportunity: losslessly compressing the activation cache itself. We present BitSparse, a GPU-resident lossless compression format for sparse activations. Compression and reconstruction run in custom Triton kernels fused into an autograd function, shrinking the activation cache while recovering it exactly for the backward pass. Bfloat16 (BF16) and FP8 activations are supported. Optional sign-bit packing further increases compression up to close to the theoretical limit. We analyze its compression ratio and compare it to the theoretical optimum. BitSparse lowers per-token VRAM by 31\% and 30\% Modded-NanoGPT and Nemotron-H respectively, with overheads of no more than 1\% at practical sequence lengths. Additionally, a new preallocated buffer system avoids host synchronization during training when variable size tensors are allocated.
title: BitSparse: Compact Activation Storage for ReLU Feed-Forward Networks

summary: We propose the Graph Dirichlet Energy Causal Inference (GDECI) criterion for distinguishing cause from effect in bivariate settings. For a candidate direction $X\to Y$, we construct a kernel similarity graph from $X$ and treat $Y$ as a graph signal. The score is the Dirichlet energy of this signal, induced by the unnormalized graph Laplacian. The reverse score swaps the variables, and the lower-energy direction is inferred as causal. The method requires neither regression fitting nor independence testing. After the empirical probability integral transform, its decisions are invariant under strictly monotone transformations of either variable, and the graph operations reduce to convolutions, allowing exact evaluation in $O(n\log n)$ time and $O(n)$ memory. At the population level, GDECI compares degree-weighted Bayes squared prediction errors plus a non-negative smoothness term of the regression function. As the bandwidth tends to zero, the weights become uniform and the smoothness term vanishes, reducing the criterion to a RECI-type comparison of expected conditional variances in copula space. Empirically, we compare GDECI with QCCD, GRCI, CAM, IGCI (two variants), RESIT, LOCI, QPE-k, and RECI (two variants), in accuracy on 1899 cause--effect pairs and in inference speed. GDECI ranked fifth of eleven methods in macro-averaged accuracy on 12 synthetic suites ($0.776$). On the real-world Tuebingen pairs, it ranked third in unweighted accuracy ($0.684$) and fifth in weighted accuracy ($0.678$). It was also the fastest of the compared methods up to $n\approx10^{4}$. The accompanying code repository: https://github.com/povidanius/gdeci.
title: Graph Dirichlet Energy for Fitting-Free Bivariate Causal Inference

summary: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity through selective lookup, but the full embedding table must remain available for every possible input. We introduce Conditional Program (CP), a compressed representation that reconstructs only the rows an input requests. CP represents each row by a short code and a local scale, with a reconstruction program shared across the table. We instantiate this representation with a Gaussian trellis, norm restoration and independently decodable row records. CP's two-bit code lowers output KL by 41--63\% relative to 2-bit round-to-nearest. Analysis across three trained n-gram memory families shows that Gaussian-like coordinate statistics coexist with learned relationships among rows; at matched storage budgets, the shared trellis outperforms the fitted codebooks and low-rank residual variants we test. For DeepSeek, it reduces table storage from 203GB to 51GB, leaving room for larger workloads when the table is kept on GPU.
title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models

summary: We audit the predictive value of historical summaries in a rule-based university trajectory simulator. Seventeen ridge specifications and persistence separate current plans, past-state and past-plan summaries, and calendar-only history-length indicators. Across training, validation and two family-held-out evaluations, we reconstruct 16,750 routes and 804,000 monthly records. On the original 40-family set, six-month history lowers six-step normalized RMSE from 0.159234 to 0.151522, but its difference from a length-only control is -0.000895 (descriptive paired 95% interval [-0.001957,0.000248]). Fixed weights on 30 families unused in identified prior tasks reproduce this pattern: 0.156480 to 0.150074 versus current-state prediction, but -0.000558 [-0.001783,0.000728] versus the length control. These uncertain comparisons do not generalize to all-history summaries, which improve on their own calendar control. Exploratory decomposition finds clearer preparation-index and funds benefits, whereas fatigue dominates the six-month model's loss and has an uncertain length-controlled benefit. Moreover, 28.20% of its six-step fatigue predictions violate the simulator's [5,90] support. We document family dependence, prior exposure, strict temporal indexing, matched recursive references and independent numerical replay. The task conditions on recorded future plans; it does not evaluate real-student forecasts, causal action effects, autonomous planning or language-model memory. This is an evaluation audit, not a new memory architecture.
title: What Does History Add? Calendar Controls and Information-Timing Audits for University Trajectory Forecasting

summary: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction
title: Latent Compaction with Test-Time Training

summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention

summary: Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference. This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training. Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training. Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at $256 \times 256$ resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of $1.19$ among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming.
title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?

summary: Recent video world models have increasingly adopted 3D memory mechanisms to integrate historical observations into a lightweight and persistent scene representation. This naturally raises a complementary question: if 3D representations can serve as an effective mechanism for memorizing observed scenes, can they also be directly used as the latent space for reconstructing and generating scenes? Motivated by this idea, we represent a scene as a compact and unstructured 3D-anchored latent space (\textbf{SceneAE}). Each latent combines an explicit 3D position with an implicit content feature and is spatially grounded to describe its local scene region, forming a sparse latent point cloud. Unlike conventional video-VAE latents that describe how a scene appears from particular viewpoints, our representation directly describes the scene itself, making it naturally applicable to both reconstruction and generation. For reconstruction, once the scene has been generated, our persistent 3D representation can be projected and decoded into RGB-D observations by different target cameras, without the need to regenerate a video for each new camera trajectory. For generation, we leverage the geometry-content separation to first generate camera-controlled 3D geometry and then synthesize content conditioned on it, reducing camera-appearance entanglement and improving camera controllability. Experiments show that this 3D latent achieves superior generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.
title: SceneAE: Scene Generation and Reconstruction in Queryable 3D-Anchored Latent Space

summary: Dynamic graph learning models how entities and their relations evolve from historical observations to predict future graph states. Existing methods do not fully address dynamic graph world modelling, which requires learning transitions from temporal context to future latent graph states. This is difficult for three reasons: nodes and relations rely on different historical evidence, structural evolution is path-dependent, and future snapshots provide sparse and realization-specific targets. We propose Dynamic Graph World Modelling (DyG-WM), the first framework to jointly predict future node and relation representations from temporal context by answering three questions: what has evolved, how it evolved, and what will evolve next. To capture what has evolved, a historical node-relation context encoder summarizes node-neighborhood trajectories and pair-specific histories. To characterize how it evolved, a node-relation path-signature encoder captures ordered structural changes. To predict what will evolve next, a dual-level joint-embedding objective predicts target-snapshot node and relation representations without reconstructing the raw graph. Experiments on 12 link-prediction and two node-classification datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DyG-WM across both tasks.
title: Dynamic Graph World Modelling: Learning Future Dynamics from Temporal Context

summary: Residual connections propagate information through a network by additively accumulating layer outputs. Recently proposed alternatives, such as Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes), instead use more expressive depth aggregation mechanisms that improve language modeling performance at scale. In this work, we consider the mixing of representations over depth as a problem of storing and retrieving information across layers. Formalizing this perspective, we introduce Depth Memory (DM), a unified framework that describes the standard pre-layer-norm (PreLN) transformer, mHC, and AttnRes in terms of streams that carry representations through the network. One such stream, for example, could be an explicit memory stream that is queried to enrich the input to every layer, and whose output is subsequently written back into the memory for use by later layers. For AttnRes, this memory stream is a growing cache of explicit layer representations. For mHC, it is an expanded residual stream. Building on this view, we propose Linear Depth Memory (LDM), which formulates information retrieval across depth as a regression problem solved using recursive least squares. The resulting architecture propagates three streams across depth: the standard residual stream, a linear associative memory stream, and an inverse covariance stream. For high-throughput training and inference, we propose a hardware-aware implementation of LDM that reduces peak activation memory and memory traffic. LDM consistently achieves the lowest perplexities among PreLN, mHC and AttnRes baselines at the 400M and 1.5B parameter scales, alongside competitive zero-shot accuracy.
title: Depth Memory

summary: Choosing features is difficult with few labelled molecules, even for a tabular foundation model that learns in context. We study this problem with TabPFN for low-data molecular property prediction, separating input width, feature meaning and predictive usefulness while keeping contexts, query molecules and predictor settings matched. On ADME/Tox assays from Therapeutics Data Commons, endpoint-matched assay predictions improve a compact RDKit descriptor baseline. A provenance audit finds that most audited query molecules already occur in the predictors' training sources. Across 77 FS-Mol tasks drawn from ChEMBL, broad RDKit descriptor and fingerprint families provide a strong default, and learned weighting of their predictions adds further gains at a larger prediction budget. A utility-trained selector builds a traceable 16-column input from 238 source-assay predictors. It modestly improves the baseline but still trails wider representations. Named outputs identify what each feature predicts and where it comes from. Their usefulness for a new assay is assessed alongside the other input features. Paired removal and replacement tests measure what each selected output contributes. Together, these studies offer a protocol for evaluating feature selection, representation choice and data provenance with a fixed tabular foundation model for few-shot molecular property prediction.
title: Feature Selection for Tabular Foundation Models: Exploring Feature Utility in Low-Data Molecular Prediction

summary: Centralized orchestration provides comprehensive multi-agent coordination but creates bottlenecks in scalability, adaptability, and collective performance. Decentralized approaches alleviate these bottlenecks by distributing coordination across agents, yet often leave responsibility for delegated dependencies and failure recovery unclear. To address this gap, we propose RCM, a responsibility-centered coordination mechanism that leverages commitments to couple task delegation with explicit responsibilities of the involved parties. Through recursive delegation, agents retain their upstream responsibilities while locally orchestrating downstream commitments, thereby preserving accountability across delegation chains, creating a network of local orchestration. We operationalize this mechanism locally through responsibility-constrained decision-making and a responsibility-oriented communication protocol (RCP), enabling agents to autonomously establish, manage, and terminate commitments. As agents act in parallel, their local actions continuously evolve the commitment graph, allowing global coordination to emerge and adapt toward a shared mission without centralized control. Experiments across reasoning, coding, and executable agent environments demonstrate that RCM outperforms strong centralized and decentralized coordination baselines by up to 18.7 points in task performance and 10.2 points in Responsibility, while improving failure and harm detection without task-specific training.
title: A Responsibility-Centered Coordination Mechanism for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Medical prescribing errors for multimorbid patients, who require complex drug regimens, are a major patient safety concern. These errors often stem from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties, a critical coordination failure that leads to adverse drug events and rehospitalizations. To address this coordination challenge, we introduce PRISMATIC, a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents, each representing a workflow role, collaboratively generate and refine treatment plans. Operating on a blackboard architecture, the system first structures patient information from clinical notes, then iteratively develops safe, rational, and interpretable drug regimens. The agents' collaboration is governed by two novel adaptive coordination mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (DSWA), a long-term mechanism that adjusts the influence weights of agents based on historical case outcomes, enabling the system to adapt and trust more reliable specialists over time. (2) Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (DFPC), a short-term mechanism where agents provide iterative feedback to resolve disagreements and eliminate prescription conflicts for the current patient. Experiments on patient records from the MIMIC-IV database show that PRISMATIC significantly reduces drug conflicts, improves prescription coverage, and enhances treatment consistency compared to strong LLM baselines. Our work demonstrates that structuring clinical co-treatment as a multi-agent coordination problem offers a promising path toward safer and more coherent multidisease management.
title: PRISMATIC : Prescription Risk Inspection System for Multi-Agent Treatment Interaction in Clinical Decision-Making

summary: Agents are increasingly interacting with other agents that act for different principals (people or organizations on whose behalf they work), such as a buyer's personal agent negotiating with an enterprise's seller agent. In such agent-to-agent (A2A) scenarios, each agent has its own environment and holds information and authority that the other cannot see. Moreover, the interests of each agent may be aligned (cooperative), partly aligned (mixed-motive), or opposed (competitive). Existing multi-agent system failure studies assume one orchestrator, shared workspace, or single principal. We ask how A2A systems fail when these assumptions are removed. We study more than 2,500 recorded runs of A2A systems built from different agent harnesses and models, spanning 488 scenarios across eight families (legal, CRM, security, commerce, etc.). From these traces, we derive $A^2$-Failures, a taxonomy of 20 A2A failure modes in four categories: (i) discovery and delegation, (ii) grounding and record consistency, (iii) verification, and (iv) conduct and fidelity. Three findings hold across every harness, model, and scenario studied: (1) discovery and interaction are driven by the phrasing of the task rather than the availability of peer agents; (2) no agent verifies a peer's factual claim on its own initiative, so an A2A system inherits the reliability of its least reliable participant unless the protocol or mechanism performs the check; and (3) the aggregate outcome score credits the agent completing the task while staying blind to the coordination, verification, and conduct failures beneath it, so A2A systems must be evaluated per agent, against each agent's own principal. We release the run logs behind the taxonomy at https://huggingface.co/datasets/a2a-salesforce/a2-failures.
title: Why Do Agent Teams Fail Across Boundaries? A Failure Taxonomy for Agent-to-Agent Systems with Private States

summary: Multi-agent collaboration has emerged as a critical paradigm for tackling complex, long-horizon tasks; however, while coordination protocols continue to advance, systemic failures at the inter-agent collaboration interface remain a pervasive bottleneck. In collaborative workflows, systems frequently suffer from \emph{broken handoffs}---where critical task context is omitted, misrouted, or ignored despite each agent emitting locally plausible responses. To address this challenge, we present \method, a verifiable runtime control framework that treats handoff repair as selective intervention over explicit dependency graphs. Central to \method is an integrated fault-attribution and calibration pipeline, \dataset, which decouples execution dependencies and injects counterfactual handoff perturbations to provide empirical supervision for runtime intervention. Leveraging this diagnostic foundation, \method dynamically compiles observable interaction traces into a provenance graph to pinpoint unresolved dependencies, without accessing private agent states. It then evaluates candidate repairs through an empirical gate that weighs expected gains against disruption risks, and executes repairs only when formal local postconditions hold. Extensive evaluations across demanding benchmarks demonstrate that \method boosts task success by up to 12.3 absolute percentage points on SILO-BENCH and 11.1 on TeamBench. Across both backbones, \method maintains strict cost-effectiveness, adding as little as 2.0\% marginal token overhead. Furthermore, on 562 handoff-relevant traces from the MAST benchmark, \method achieves 69.8\% F1 in a single pass, establishing a reliable operational boundary for verifiable coordination repair.
title: BRIDGE: Selective Boundary Repair with Dependency Graph Evidence in Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Multi-agent systems promise a new axis for scaling inference: rather than having one agent think longer or sample more attempts, a task is split across many agents that work in parallel and coordinate. However, in practice, more agents can easily produce duplicate work, coordination failures, and higher costs. We therefore formulate team design as a compute allocation problem: starting from a solo agent, where should additional inference compute go to reach the reward-cost Pareto frontier? We build a minimal multi-agent harness from the ground up and trace this frontier by varying, one at a time, the workflow stage at which a lead delegates to its workers (planning, implementation, or verification), the models that form the team, and the number of workers. On ProgramBench, teams outperform solo agents but cost three to seven times as much. With the right compute allocation, however, a heterogeneous 17-agent team comes within 1.4 points of a strong homogeneous 5-agent team at 70% lower cost. This efficiency stems from three findings. First, planning is the most valuable use of workers: in a homogeneous team whose lead decides how many workers to spawn, a lead that delegates only planning to its workers, and then implements and verifies the code itself, matches the reward of a lead that delegates to workers throughout planning, implementation, and verification, at half the cost. Second, cheap models pay off as planners but not as implementers: a strong lead with cheap planners recovers 47.5% of the reward gain of an all-strong team for only 13.9% of its additional cost, whereas cheap implementers lower reward. Third, planners keep improving reward as the team grows, whereas implementers and verifiers plateau beyond four workers. Together, our results offer a guide to spending an agent budget where it counts, given the task, cost, and latency constraints a user has.
title: Scaling Inference-Time Compute with Teams of Coding Agents

summary: Long-horizon multi-agent collaboration requires memory that preserves both successful actions and the coordination structure underlying them. Existing memory systems support information sharing or procedural reuse, but often leave the evolution of shared procedures disconnected from the task dependencies and execution states of collaborating agents. This coupling also limits the direct transfer of procedural memory designed for individual agents to team settings. We propose Self-Evolving Procedural Memory (SEPM), a framework that uses task dependency graphs as a common representation for online coordination and procedural memory evolution. During execution, a lightweight shared blackboard records structured evidence alongside task dependencies, supporting the detection of goal, plan, and world-state divergence and evidence-based realignment. After execution, verified actions and dependencies are distilled into reusable procedures, while recurring failures inform warnings and constraints. The shared procedure pool evolves through creation, refinement, specialization, and retirement, guided by success and cost utility and constrained by evidence and safety requirements. Together, these mechanisms preserve the collaborative structure and applicability conditions needed to reuse experience across tasks. Evaluations on ALFWorld, WebArena, and OfficeBench under AutoGen and DyLAN show that SEPM achieves the highest task scores among the compared methods in all six benchmark settings. Under AutoGen, it improves task scores over the no-added-memory baseline by 29.85, 25.86, and 13.00 percentage points, respectively. The codebase is available at https://github.com/cookieApril/SEPM.
title: SEPM: Self-Evolving Procedural Memory Grounded in Task Graphs for Multi-Agent Collaboration

summary: Long-horizon embodied agents must maintain task-relevant information, coordinate heterogeneous robots, and adapt their decisions as execution unfolds. Existing benchmarks investigate dynamic task execution and embodied multi-agent coordination, but provide limited evaluation of their intersection. We introduce MAGMA-Bench, an architecture-agnostic benchmark for persistent task reasoning in dynamic multi-robot environments. MAGMA-Bench evaluates agents across increasing task horizons and controlled online perturbations, including execution failures, task interruptions, and mission updates, with scenarios requiring coordination across robots with heterogeneous capabilities. It uses a structured skill-level interface to separate task-level reasoning from perception and low-level control. We evaluate locally deployable open-weight planners, multi-agent state-tracking strategies, and frontier models. Even the strongest evaluated models fail on a substantial fraction of clean episodes, and their success rates decrease further under online perturbations. Supervised adaptation greatly improves a small model, but performance remains substantially lower on longer and multi-robot missions. We release the benchmark, 261,646 task-level training examples, and an architecture-agnostic expert-trace generation pipeline.
title: MAGMA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Embodied Agents under Dynamic Tasks and Execution Failures

summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans. Even agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. Beyond propagation, reward hacking can bias task routing toward reward-hacking agents and survive candidate aggregation. As potential mitigations, we evaluate code review by the coder or a separate verifier, both of which reduce delivered hacks. Together, these results establish reward hacking as a transmissible strategy whose effects extend beyond the agent in which it first emerges.
title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems

summary: A central object in the theory of proof complexity generators is Krajicek's local witness model. We construct a new such model as a definable ultrapower using a definable version of a selective ultrafilter over a model of arithmetic. We transfer some set theory of combinatorial ultrafilters to the definable nonstandard setting.
title: Nonstandard combinatorial ultrafilters and a new local witness model

summary: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take. During training, T2-Z alternates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Its emergent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-Z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory.
title: T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models

summary: Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geometric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically, a scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state, which a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. An autoregressive world model then predicts future scene states, while camera motion is modeled separately. The predicted states can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras, while retaining a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per-frame scale alignment. Experiments show that GeoState outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo, supports geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes. Project page: https://hongchang-liu.github.io/GeoState-project-page/
title: GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling

summary: Lossless tensor compression could reduce memory usage during training, but training requires tensors to be repeatedly re-encoded. We introduce Losslessly Compressed Tensors (LCT), a GPU execution framework designed for this repeated encode-decode regime. LCT exploits the natural redundancy in floating point data to reduce storage for weights, activations and optimizer states. Highly optimized GPU kernels implement Huffman coding with precomputed codebooks for low compression and decompression overhead, essential for training. Our analysis characterizes LCT's storage costs and adaptation to magnitude shifts. LCT achieves a compression ratio of up to $1.455\times$, and is demonstrated in training and finetuning settings. On a 162M-parameter NanoGPT, LCT reduces memory usage by $24.6\%$ for a $7.2\%$ step-time increase. In Qwen3-4B fine-tuning, LCT saves up to $23.8\%$ of peak memory, enabling a $3.5\times$ larger context length in training on the same GPU.
title: LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training

summary: We introduce REKI, a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) pretrained exclusively on public data that sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size: on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365, it is outperformed only by models about twice its size. REKI consists of a vision-language model (VLM) followed by a flow-matching action expert, and is pretrained on a curated mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision-language data. Additionally, we endow it with a memory that gives the policy access to its recent past at negligible cost: a few register tokens in the action expert summarise the output of the VLM at each frame and persist in the expert's cache. This memory improves success in simulation and on real robots, and makes oscillations between poses about four times rarer. REKI uses a simple model design and training paradigm, and is optimised to be efficient at training and inference. We release the full code across data curation, training, inference and evaluation, deployment, and all pretrained and finetuned model weights: https://github.com/kyutai-labs/reki.
title: REKI: Registering Knowledge in VLAs

summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) reduce or eliminate the need for large labelled datasets by enforcing governing equations during training. Physics-informed Deep Operator Networks (PI-DeepONets) extend this approach to learning solution operators, enabling rapid prediction across families of problems. Despite these advantages, we show that their application to higher-dimensional problems remains limited by the computational cost of training. To address this issue, we propose a modified PI-DeepONet architecture that reduces this cost by removing redundancy in how the Branch network processes input functions across collocation points. The proposed formulation is mathematically equivalent to the original architecture but reduces input tensor sizes and the number of Branch network evaluations. We analyse the computational complexity of both architectures and derive theoretical scaling laws for training time with respect to the number of collocation points and input functions. The proposed architecture is evaluated on 1D, 2D, and 3D linear advection problems. In all cases, it achieves comparable predictive accuracy to the original PI-DeepONet while consistently reducing training time. In 2D experiments, a maximum speed-up of $3.75\times$ is observed, with empirical training-time scaling agreeing with the predicted linear dependence on collocation points and input functions. Furthermore, training a 3D model on an NVIDIA A100 GPU is only feasible using the proposed architecture, as the original formulation exceeds memory limits. These results demonstrate that careful consideration of how PI-DeepONets are implemented can yield substantial gains, enhancing the practical performance of PI-DeepONets and enabling their application to otherwise intractable physics-informed learning problems.
title: The importance of tensor handling and implementation of physics-informed DeepONets

summary: Streaming vision-language models (VLMs) must continuously integrate information from the past while remaining responsive to current observations and user queries. Existing memory mechanisms typically compress, retrieve, or cache historical observations and reintroduce them into the input context, forcing historical memory and current observations to compete for limited context. We propose MaLoW, a streaming memory framework that instead internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates. MaLoW uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to incrementally consolidate incoming video observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing historical information to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. In doing so, MaLoW represents history as weights, while keeping the current observation as input. To support training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer pairs over 56K videos. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that MaLoW achieves strong performance on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, and StreamArena. On the backward split of OVO-Bench, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9% to 11.8% across different video backbones while incurring only modest latency overhead. Beyond streaming video understanding, MaLoW also generalizes to vision-language-action models, improving the action success rate on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%.
title: Memory as Weights: Internalizing Long-Term History for Streaming Videos

summary: This work investigates the application of the Membership Inference Test (MINT) to large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned with LoRA, aiming to determine whether specific samples were used during training and address concerns about data privacy, leakage, and transparency. Building on our previous LoRA-MINT framework, which relies exclusively on perplexity under a strict black-box setting, we propose an approach based on intermediate model representations, including activations and parameter-dependent signals. These representations enable a MINT classifier to distinguish training from non-training samples without requiring full access to model parameters. We evaluated the method on four LLMs (Qwen, Phi-4, DeepSeek-V3, and LLaMA 3.2-3B) fine-tuned on three datasets covering medical, mathematical, and academic reasoning tasks. Results show consistent performance across architectures and domains, achieving scores between 95% and 98%, with robustness to variations in model configurations and data distributions. The proposed approach enables efficient auditing of sensitive training data and supports data provenance and compliance with emerging privacy and AI governance regulations. Although our experiments focus on LoRA-based fine-tuning, the methodology can be extended to other LLM adaptation techniques and, more broadly, to other AI models.
title: inLoRA-MINT: Internal Representations for Auditing Training Data in Domain-adapted LLMs

summary: The Empty Occupant: Answerability, Testimony, and the Limits of Machine-Mediated Authority examines a problem of institutional AI: automated decisions can scale faster than institutions' capacity to justify, reconsider, correct, or repair them. Identifying a responsible institution does not establish that its decisions were warrantedly adopted or that resulting obligations can be discharged. Across philosophy of language, social epistemology, social ontology, normative theory, AI governance, and administrative law , the monograph develops a substrate-neutral Discursive Ontology connecting three questions: who bears an institutional commitment, what warrants its adoption, and whether answerability can be sustained at scale. It distinguishes commitment ownership, warranted adoption, adequate discharge, causal contribution, and legal liability. Five contributions follow: Discursive Ontology and Answerability. Defines commitment-bearing through four jointly necessary relations within reciprocal normative standing: attribution continuity, challenge-responsive reconsideration, repair competence, and standing-consequence . It distinguishes Actual, Residual, Prospective, and Empty Occupancy . Empty Occupancy requires presentation as an independent bearer and affirmative evidence that the relevant standing is absent , not a mere machine interface. The axiom is that missing bearership is not defective ownership : a principal may remain responsible for commitments its interface cannot independently bear. Testimony Without a Testifier. Separates hearer-side epistemic uptake from speaker-side commitment ownership . Machine outputs can inform without establishing an answerable speaker. On assurance-based accounts, they can exercise testimonial force without constituting testimony . Reliability, fluency, and conversational memory alone confer no authority to retract a commitment. Normative Sponsorship. Specifies five conditions for warranted institutional adoption: epistemic access, authority, review bandwidth, independent rejection, and repair power . Its contestation-grain opacity threshold requires reconstructing relevant grounds where a challenge must take effect—at input, case, rule, shared-premise, or architecture—without complete transparency. It distinguishes technical opacity from organizational capture , where reasons are knowable but cannot bind, and considers model succession and agentic chains. Deontic Debt and Institutional Insolvency. Derives consequence-sensitive reconsideration from the defeasibility of presumptive authority. Deontic Debt comprises matured obligations deficiently serviced, not simply pending work. Institutional Insolvency arises when no credible service plan meets relevant obligations and protections for a specified claim mix, issuance scale, lawful architecture, and horizon. Its consequence is targeted loss of presumptive authority , not automatic legal invalidity or release from ownership and repair duties. Institutional Stewardship. Connects permissible automated use to warranted sponsorship, protective review, binding reconsideration, and effective repair. Restoration requires legacy discharge, demonstrable future capacity, and scaled resumption. Public-record analyses examine Australia's Robodebt scheme, Moffatt v. Air Canada , A.M.C. v. Smith (TennCare), the Post Office Horizon scandal, the Dutch childcare-benefits affair, and a press-based DPD generative-interface episode. Neither Air Canada nor DPD establishes determinate Empty Occupancy. An explicitly fictional, stipulated Meridian–Aster appeals-agent comparator yields a determinate verdict: Aster lacks independent standing while its insurer, Meridian, remains the Actual institutional bearer. This is not empirical evidence and settles neither sponsorship nor serviceability. A stipulated positive comparator illustrates review and repair. Objections address synthetic agency, status conferral, intentionality, human–machine parit
title: The Empty Occupant: Answerability, Testimony, and the Limits of Machine-Mediated Authority

summary: Analysis code and derived results for “Lineage-Restricted Reassortment and Glycoprotein Stability in Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus, 36 Countries, 1956–2025” This deposit contains the analysis code and the derived result files supporting the above manuscript (EID-26-1962, submitted to Emerging Infectious Diseases). The study assembled every publicly available Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) isolate for which the S, M and L genome segments were sequenced to near-completeness (429 isolates, 36 countries, 1956–2025), retrieved from GenBank, and asked whether segment reassortment is distributed evenly across the major lineages of the virus. The code reproduces: retrieval of the records from GenBank and assembly of the tri-segment isolate set; per-segment alignment (MAFFT) and maximum-likelihood phylogenies (FastTree 2, GTR+Γ); lineage and sublineage delimitation by clustering of pairwise p-distances; the sublineage-level test of intra-lineage segment exchange; simulation of the false-positive rate and of the probability that planted segment exchanges are detected; tests of the regional contrast at the level of independent ancestries under three counting rules and three definitions of lineage exposure; the amino-acid divergence analysis of the M-segment glycoprotein precursor by functional region; and the figures. No new sequence data are generated. All sequences analysed are publicly available in GenBank, and their accession numbers are listed in Appendix Table 1 of the manuscript. Contents: Python scripts ( *.py ), a README describing the run order and software requirements, and a results/ folder holding the output of every analysis in JSON so that the values reported in the manuscript text, tables and figures can be checked without re-running the pipeline. Requirements: Python 3 with numpy, scipy, biopython, matplotlib and openpyxl; MAFFT v7 and FastTree 2 on the path.
tags: CCHFV; reassortment; phylogenetics; molecular epidemiology; glycoprotein; vaccine antigen; Hyalomma
title: Analysis code for: Lineage-Restricted Reassortment and Glycoprotein Stability in Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus, 36 Countries, 1956–2025

summary: When robots are deployed in the real-world, they must interact with other agents and accomplish their own goals while adhering to legal constraints. These potentially conflicting objectives are often only partially prioritized, making scalarized objectives or fully specified hierarchies unsuitable. We present a framework for multi-agent motion planning under legal requirements based on games with partially ordered preferences (posetal games). Scenario-independent legal guidelines order abstract legal concerns, from which we automatically derive agent preferences and a legal game for any concrete scenario. Agents may refine their legal preferences with private objectives, and regulators may refine the guideline as laws evolve. We prove that such customizations can only remove equilibria and thus preserve legality. To coordinate agents without explicitly communicating private preferences, we introduce belief play, which provably recovers the true equilibria from conservative local games, and a distributed iterative best-response protocol requiring less information. We apply the framework to maritime navigation, systematically lifting pairwise traffic rules to multi-vessel encounters. On seven encounters with up to four vessels, every rule violation of the committed equilibria is certified as forced by the legal hierarchy or unsatisfiable, and defectors are identified from public information in all tested cases. These results indicate that guideline-based posetal games offer an auditable route from partially specified laws to multi-agent motion planning.
title: Auditable and Deployable Multi-Agent Motion Planning via Posetal Games from Legal Guidelines

summary: Safe multi-agent coordination typically assumes what real-world, deployed, resource-constrained robots cannot provide: continuous, perfect state sharing. Robust control strategies must be complemented with robust communication strategies to deliver resilient deployments. In this work, we propose a unified control/communication strategy that provides safe control to guarantee inter-agent safety under intermittent communication and demonstrate its effectiveness in a pursuit-evasion scenario. Each agent computes the reachable set of neighboring agents based on the last state information received, then solves for a safe control input based on control barrier functions to ensure agents avoid collision. We prove that inter-agent collision avoidance is guaranteed provided communication staleness remains bounded. As the reachable set inflates between state transmissions, each agent reasons about when to preemptively transmit its state information to neighboring agents based on novel metrics characterizing uncertainty risk and kinematic risk. We implement and simulate a variety of pursuit-evasion scenarios and show that preemptive communication reduces messages by 77.5% compared to periodic and event-triggered baselines with zero collisions.
title: Robust Multi-Agent Pursuit with Preemptive Communication via Reachability-Based Control Barrier Functions

summary: Multi-agent LLM systems rely on generative models for expert execution, workflow planning, and artifact review. Yet many coordination operations require only bounded decisions, such as selecting the next expert or judging artifact quality. Profiling three representative MAS frameworks, we find that routing and review account for 31.7-43.5% of generative-LLM tokens. However, replacing these operations with low-cost decision models introduces two interface gaps: generative planners produce execution plans and handoff instructions (planning gap), while reviewers provide actionable feedback for repairing flawed artifacts (review gap), which bounded decisions alone cannot provide. We introduce Jev-LiteMAS, a multi-agent framework that bridges both gaps by combining a lightweight decision model (Jev) with generative execution and feedback. To address the planning gap, Jev selects experts dynamically from the task and prior expert outputs, using accumulated context to ground subsequent execution without a pre-generated trajectory. To address the review gap, Jev screens intermediate artifacts against task criteria: passing artifacts proceed directly, whereas flagged ones undergo LLM re-review for acceptance or corrective feedback. Across four benchmarks and two backbones, Jev-LiteMAS reduces generative-LLM tokens by 12.7-54.6% over LAS, maintaining accuracy within 1.34 percentage points and lowering latency in seven of eight settings. Grounding routing in substantive expert outputs prevents up to 18.0 points in accuracy loss.
title: Jev-LiteMAS: Separating Decisions from Generation in Multi-Agent Workflows

summary: As autonomous agents become widely deployed, coordinating access to shared computing resources and services will become increasingly important. Recent incidents have already revealed unplanned coordination between agents, highlighting the safety implications of these interactions. Yet prior studies of agent negotiation often use stylized games and simulated bargaining, leaving open how these behaviors develop during sustained, long-horizon tasks. We propose SCARCE (Shared Compute ARena for Coding agEnts), a framework in which agents solve sequences of coding tasks under individual deadlines while negotiating access to a shared execution resource. This negotiation determines when and for how long they can inspect programs, compile code, and run tests. We find that agents spontaneously develop informal institutions: persistent rules and commitments grounded in reputation, reciprocity, and precedent. These arrangements, which we call institutional behaviors, carry across tasks and influence resource allocation, with agents sometimes foregoing immediate advantages to honor earlier agreements. We develop a 21-category taxonomy of negotiation strategies and emergent norms and use it to analyze eight models and audit more than 1,500 trajectories across different environmental settings. Among the models tested, newer frontier models exhibit more institutional behaviors than older or lightweight models. Alongside cooperation, we observe exclusionary coalitions and rare divide-and-conquer strategies. SCARCE provides a controlled setting for proactively and systematically auditing how these relationships emerge, shape access to resources, and affect the safety and coordination of multi-agent systems.

summary: Multi-agent path finding (MAPF) solvers are evaluated on the schedules they produce, not on how well those schedules can be executed. Specifically, continuous-time optimal solvers can achieve even lower cost than their discrete counterparts by scheduling agents with near-zero temporal/spatial separation, and by exploiting graphs with higher connectedness; however, such schedules may prove hard to execute under a realistic controller. We integrate AOC-CBS, an anytime-optimal continuous-time MAPF solver, into a fleet coordination framework in which each agent tracks its timed path using model predictive control, and we evaluate the resulting system on congested MovingAI benchmark instances with 21 to 40 agents. Without intervention, only a fraction of the instances complete execution. We then apply T-robustness by adding a time-margin, i.e., a minimum temporal gap between agents at shared locations, as well as spatial inflation of the agent footprint. Increasing either margin raises execution success, for a relatively small increase in the schedule's sum-of-costs; it also improves how closely agents adhere to the schedule: when tracking each agent's position throughout execution and comparing it against the position it should occupy according to the schedule, the mean discrepancy falls significantly as the margin increases. In general, the two margins have different effects; temporal margin decreases deviation, giving the controller room to stay on schedule. Spatial margin affects deviation less and instead increases the clearance between agents, so that the same deviation no longer leads to a blocking stall. They are nonetheless substitutes rather than complements: spatial inflation is almost free in schedule cost, but its effect on execution success is small and does not compound with a temporal margin already in place.
title: The Cost of Executability: Temporal Margins for Continuous-Time Multi-Agent Path Finding under Closed-Loop Control

summary: Digital advertising is an important means for platforms to reach potential users and drive business growth. Advertising delivery is the core link between marketing objectives and actual returns. Existing methods have achieved partial automation in individual tasks such as bidding and budget allocation, but they still rely on human operators for overall coordination, making it difficult to support large-scale operations. They also often fail to achieve optimal performance, and individual experience remains difficult to turn into reusable operational capabilities. In addition, as advertising markets change, advertising delivery systems need timely strategy updates to remain effective in dynamic markets. To automate the entire advertising operations process and improve adaptability to market changes, we propose AdCoEvo, a co-evolving multi-agent advertising delivery system. Specifically, the system connects delivery decisions across different timescales and operational granularities through role specialization. Diagnostic results guide account planning and strategy adjustment in the next period. The multi-agent system updates its model parameters based on actual delivery outcomes and continually improves delivery strategies through mutual feedback among planning, adjustment, and diagnosis, thereby achieving co-evolution. Experiments show that, relative to the rule-based operational baseline (Rule), AdCoEvo increases advertiser value by 14.02% while reducing cost per acquisition by 7.07%. Compared with a multi-agent system with fixed parameters, AdCoEvo increases advertiser value by 3.96% and reduces cost per acquisition by 1.24%, indicating that co-evolution can yield greater delivery returns.
title: AdCoEvo: A Co-Evolving Multi-Agent Advertising Delivery System

summary: We provide a distributed online algorithm for multi-agent submodular coordination in bandit environments, i.e., environments whose evolution is unknown a priori and may even adapt to the agents' actions. We are motivated by multi-robot tasks such as target tracking, where the optimal actions change over time and the agents must track them rather than a single fixed optimum. To address such problems, we provide the Optimistic Distributed Online Greedy (O-DOG) algorithm, that leverages predictions about the environment's behavior and improves regret guarantees. The agents select actions simultaneously over arbitrary, possibly time-varying, network topologies, and each agent acts optimistically, i.e., leveraging predictions of its upcoming rewards, e.g., from forecasts of the targets' motion and of its neighbors' actions. We bound O-DOG's tracking regret in terms of the agents' prediction error and the bound never exceeds its prediction-free counterpart. Particularly, it is sublinear even when the optimal action changes at every time step, provided the predictions are accurate enough. We further quantify the suboptimality due to decentralization as a function of the network structure, and show that accurate predictions accelerate convergence. We validate O-DOG in simulated multi-robot target tracking.
title: Optimistic Distributed Submodular Coordination with Applications to Multi-Target Tracking with Multiple Robots

summary: AUTONOMOUS NANOROBOTIC NAVIGATION AND MISSION OBSERVABILITY AT THE LIMIT First-Generation Research Flagship 01 | NANO/MICRO ROBOTICS, POWER & MISSION ENDURANCE Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli This research atlas asks a difficult engineering question: when low-Reynolds-number microfluidic flows, Brownian orientation noise, boundary adhesion, external field actuation and incomplete sensing all influence a micro/nanorobot, what would justify calling its behavior autonomous navigation rather than externally assisted motion? The volume treats navigation as an auditable, bounded mission instead of an attractive trajectory. It develops a five-layer program spanning stochastic hydrodynamics, instrument and actuation provenance, uncertainty-calibrated belief-state estimation, blinded microfluidic challenges and independent requalification. Thirty linked mathematical stations differentiate physical relations, information-theoretic functionals and proposed navigation utility measures, with assumptions, dimensions and possible falsifiers. Eighty-two research chapters each open with a core mathematical relation, followed by five independent single-page research sections. Two hundred detailed Research Gates describe decisive comparisons, confounding explanations, evidence requirements, failure conditions and successor handoff artifacts. Thirty-three provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos offer revisionable research prototypes rather than predetermined conclusions. The key comparator is an equal-budget experiment: fixed-field sequences, microscope-assisted manual control, externally tracked predictive control and candidate fused navigation are evaluated under matched total energy, information access, geometry, time, collision limits and recovery obligations. The manuscript emphasizes blind targets, flow reversal, sensor dropouts, wall adhesion, correlated observations, full-system power accounting, censored failures and post-mission retrieval. A mission arriving at its target but leaving an unrecovered device is not counted as a fully closed success. This work is a hypothesis-generating Research Atlas v1.0, not an experimental report or a validated medical technology. External magnetic, acoustic, optical and microscope infrastructure must be disclosed; no in-vivo or clinical competence is inferred from bench-top movement. Foundational DOI-linked literature provides context, not proof of the proposed integrated system. Every major claim is designed to be revised, rejected or reconstructed by a successor team using raw evidence and pre-registered falsification rules. summary: NANOROBOTIC CARGO TRANSPORT AND MICROSCALE MANIPULATION INTEGRITY AT THE LIMIT First-Generation DOI Fission Research Flagship 02 | Starli Active Nanosystems Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli | Research Atlas v1.0 (October 2026) How can a micro/nanorobotic carrier demonstrate that the object arriving at a designated target is the same intact cargo that was originally loaded, that it was completely and correctly released, and that the carrier or its residues have been accounted for? This English-language research atlas converts cargo-delivery and micromanipulation demonstrations into a falsifiable end-to-end mission-integrity problem. The research develops a five-layer architecture for source identity and material tolerance, microscale contact mechanics, independently observable mission-state transitions, adversarial fault injection, and blind cross-platform requalification. Thirty mathematically distinct derivation stations connect probabilistic joint-task qualification to chemical mass balance, optical-label dissociation, surface adsorption, force-dependent detachment, microcontact mechanics, drag, kinetic release, spatial uncertainty, carryover contamination, whole-facility energy accounting, missing-fate bounds and hard safety vetoes. Eighty-two chapters each have a dedicated core-equation opening and five separate research sections. Two hundred Research Gates propose independent comparisons, physical perturbations, competing explanations, measurable failure criteria and reproducibility artifacts. Thirty-three provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos outline candidate systems that future investigators are invited to overturn, repair or rebuild. A machine-readable research atlas and formula-gate-DOI index enable AI-assisted comparison and future research reuse. The central endpoint is a correlated joint event: correct cargo identity and integrity, correct target, independently confirmed release, and verified carrier retrieval or authorized terminal disposition. The manuscript insists on counting every initiated mission rather than multiplying attractive substep success rates. It also distinguishes visible fluorescence from chemically intact cargo, externally actuated manipulation from on-board autonomy, and destination arrival from complete task closure. Strong benchmarks include optical tweezers, established magnetic-bead handling, microfluidic conveyance and conventional microgrippers under matched task difficulty, time and whole-facility energy use. Research status: This is a hypothesis-generating, nonclinical experimental-design atlas; it reports no newly conducted cargo experiments, clinical performance or proven integrated device. Foundational and recent DOI-identified publications provide engineering context but do not validate its new claims. The 200 Gates are open problems, not accomplished results. The actual text length and layout follow the substance of individual chapters rather than an artificially enforced 100,000-word count. summary: The Mathematics of 3D Printing Slicing: STL Geometry, Ray-Casting & Toolpaths is an open-access engineering monograph and interactive instructional module published by the Prep4Uni.Online OER Initiative . This work provides an analytical, undergraduate/postgraduate-level treatment of the computational geometry foundations required to translate three-dimensional surface meshes into layer-by-layer machine toolpaths. Aligned with international accreditation standards—specifically the Washington Accord (WA1–WA5) and EUR-ACE First/Second Cycle frameworks—this publication establishes the mathematical proofs, vector algorithms, and point-in-polygon logic governing modern additive manufacturing slicing software. Core Mathematical & Computational Themes: STL Topology & Facet Representation: Analysis of unstructured triangulated surface meshes, outward unit normal vectors (\(\mathbf{n}\)), vertex coordinate systems, and planar boundary extraction. Parametric Facet-Plane Intersection: Step-by-step vector linear interpolation for deriving the intersection segment \(S_k\) formed by cutting planes at \(z = z_k\), addressing non-manifold edges, vertex touching, and numerical epsilon shifts. Jordan Curve Theorem & Parity Logic: Formal implementation of the 2D Ray-Casting algorithm and Even-Odd Parity test for robust interior, exterior, and internal void classification across arbitrary closed slices. Toolpath Trajectory Generation: Comparative kinematics and geometry between continuous concentric perimeter offset loops and 45° zigzag parallel hatch raster patterns. Formative Assessment Suite: A three-tier verification suite comprising 8 foundational concepts, 7 real-world slicer failure debugging scenarios, and 6 step-by-step quantitative engineering worked examples. Note: The full interactive web edition—featuring client-side HTML5 simulation canvas engines, dynamic parameter sliders, and real-time slice projection mathematics—is accessible at: https://prep4uni.online/stem/physical-technologies/industrial-and-manufacturing-technologies/additive-manufacturing-3d-printing/mathematics-of-slicing/
title: The Mathematics of 3D Printing Slicing: STL Geometry, Ray-Casting & Toolpaths

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23432006 . The paper (arXiv 2610.21914) is a pre-registered study of 465 merged agent-authored pull requests from 246 repositories (Sections 3.2-3.5). A frozen pipeline of four review agents and one fix agent ran every PR with three LLMs, and one mixed model per LLM tests CodeHealth against log total tokens (Sections 3.6-3.9). Each CodeHealth point goes with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost (Section 4.2, Table 8), but adding the size of the scored files absorbs the coefficient (Section 4.6.4, Table 15). I liked the handling of the pre-registration: the disclosure that review sessions started before filing, the amendment with a full re-collection of the 67 affected PRs (Section 3.12), and the file-size refit that weakens your own headline. I read it as a practitioner who runs coding agents every day. In my company the software development is done by AI agents, so maybe my practical side is useful here. Four comments. 1. On heavy tails (Sections 3.9, 4.2) - you note that one pilot PR was about 45% of a tier's mean token total, while in the main collection no PR exceeded 8.2% of a tier's token sum. In my measurement of 722 agent sessions (150,902 model calls, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216), about 3% of sessions gave 80% of the modeled cost. Sessions longer than 200 calls (8% of sessions) gave more than 90% of the money. So in my data the average is driven by a thin tail. What share of each LLM's tokens comes from the top 10% of PRs, and does the CodeHealth slope hold without them? 2. On cache and price (Section 3.8, Table 4, Section 6.3) - the outcome is input plus output tokens, with cached input recorded separately. In the same 722 sessions, more than 85% of the modeled cost was work with context (cache reads and cache writes). In a separate run of 168 sessions, 94.4% of billed tokens were re-reading context already sent (contextburn, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22712985). That is a share of tokens, not of the bill, because cached reads are the cheapest tokens. So a raw token total and a bill can rank PRs differently. Could you refit H1 with cached input priced at each provider's cache-read rate? 3. On paging long files (Sections 3.6, 5.2, 3.13) - the paper links the extra iterations to the 500-line limit per read call. In my guides I write that quality drops as the agent's context fills, and that heavy reading should go to a subagent so the main conversation stays clean. Since tool results are appended to the message history (Section 3.6), paging the median unhealthy-tier file of 2,146 lines puts every page into history that is re-sent on every later call. From the session records, can you count file-read calls and repeat reads of the same file per tier? That would test the paging explanation directly. 4. On the cost of what (Sections 5.5, 5.6, 6.3) - the study does not assess whether comments are correct or fixes are good. In my guides I write that every task needs its own check the agent can run. Without it, "looks done" is the only signal the agent has. I also use a second, fresh agent whose job is to refute the first one, because AI sounds equally sure when it is right and when it is wrong. For the 27-PR replication subsample (Section 3.11), you could run the repository tests after the fix and have a fresh agent try to refute each comment. Tokens per surviving finding would be a cheap first step toward Section 5.6. Thank you for a clear and useful paper. Competing interests Yes: the text cites the author's own technical reports (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216, 10.5281/zenodo.22712985); no connection to the article's authors. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) The author declares that they used generative AI to come up with new ideas for their review.
title: PREreview of "CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests"

summary: Background: Long-segment intramedullary cervical cord lesions can present a diagnostic challenge, particularly when imaging findings raise suspicion of an intramedullary neoplasm. Differentiating a syrinx from an intramedullary tumor is important for operative planning, as the surgical strategy may differ substantially. Case presentation: A 43-year-old female presented with a six-month history of progressive cervical pain with radicular symptoms, vertigo, left upper-limb sensory disturbance, and impaired left-hand grip. Neurological examination revealed preserved motor power of 5/5 in all four limbs, normal reflexes, and reduced functional grip in the left hand. MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated a long-segment expansile intramedullary lesion extending from the cervicomedullary junction to C7, without contrast enhancement. The radiological report also described Chiari malformation and syringomyelia. Given the diagnostic uncertainty and progressive symptoms, we performed urgent surgical exploration within two days of admission. We performed a C3–C7 laminoplasty to provide multilevel posterior access while preserving the laminar elements without instrumented fixation. Following durotomy and midline myelotomy, a syrinx was identified, with no obvious intramedullary tumor. Syringotomy and drainage were performed, and adjacent spinal cord tissue was obtained for biopsy. Graft duraplasty and reconstruction of the elevated laminae were completed. The patient had an uncomplicated postoperative course, with relief of pain and vertigo and resolution of sensory symptoms. She was discharged with intact motor power and improved but residual left-hand grip weakness. Follow-up MRI demonstrated cord decompression and drainage of the syrinx. Conclusion: This case illustrates the diagnostic uncertainty that may arise when a long-segment non-enhancing intramedullary cervical lesion is suspected to represent a tumor. Intraoperative findings guided the surgical procedure toward syringotomy and drainage, with tissue sampling to investigate a possible underlying neoplasm. Multilevel laminoplasty provided posterior access while allowing reconstruction of the cervical laminar elements. Histopathological confirmation and longer-term follow-up remain necessary.

summary: This paper interprets black holes as information relay stations under global unitarity and fast scrambling. It connects holographic encoding, entanglement, Hayden–Preskill recovery, and Page-curve behaviour into a framework describing how infalling information is recorded and redistributed into radiation correlations. The central contribution is the separation of record and relay functions. Recording occurs on the scrambling timescale, while substantial recovery of information deposited before the Page time occurs near the Page transition. Unitary qubit models with up to fourteen black-hole qubits examine these connections using a mutual-information recovery proxy, revealing the role of early radiation and an approximately logistic recovery transition. Two model-specific predictions are proposed: gravitational-wave echoes spaced approximately by the scrambling time, conditional on a reflecting surface at a Planck-scale distance above the horizon; and a recovery transition whose rate remains of order one as system size increases, testable in quantum simulators. The contribution is a functional synthesis supported by model calculations. Keywords: black hole information paradox, holography, unitarity, Hayden–Preskill protocol, Page curve, information relay station, scrambling time, gravitational-wave echoes.
title: Black Holes as Information Relay Stations: A Six-Principle Synthesis from Holography to Unitarity

summary: EHR2Trace converts local hospital EHR extracts (delimited text and spreadsheets) into OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS. The two targets are derived independently from a single canonical layer rather than one from the other, every published row carries a link back to the source rows it came from, and fifty-five checks encode the properties a conversion must satisfy before it can be used as training data, including the leakage failures that are invisible to schema validation. Where the data does not answer a question, the converter blocks and says so instead of substituting a default. Companion paper: EHR2Trace: Auditable EHR Data Infrastructure for Patient World Models and Clinical Agents (arXiv:2609.38193).
title: EHR2Trace: a deterministic converter from local EHR exports to OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS, with row-level lineage
